hints: Start by thinking about what arrives at the end of the motor neurone and what that electrical signal must do to the presynaptic membrane.
Recall which ion enters the presynaptic knob when voltage-gated channels open, and what this ion causes vesicles to do.
Think about what chemical is stored in those vesicles and how it gets into the synaptic cleft to reach the muscle.
Focus on the motor end plate on the sarcolemma - what does the chemical bind to, and which ion then enters the muscle fibre?
Consider why depolarisation cannot stay only at the surface if the whole thick fibre must contract at once - which narrow tubules carry it inwards?
Link that inward spread of depolarisation to the store of calcium ions inside the muscle - which organelle membrane is depolarised next?

walkthrough:
Start at the Neuromuscular Junction - Nerve to Chemical Signal**
An action potential arrives and depolarises the presynaptic membrane of the motor neurone. This opens voltage-gated calcium ion channels, so Ca2+ diffuse into the presynaptic knob. Calcium is the trigger for vesicles containing acetylcholine (ACh) to fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release ACh by exocytosis into the synaptic cleft.

Convert Chemical Back to Electrical in Muscle**
ACh diffuses across the cleft and binds to specific receptors on the sarcolemma at the motor end plate. This opens sodium ion channels, so Na+ rush into the sarcoplasm. The influx of positive ions depolarises the muscle cell surface membrane, creating an end-plate potential that triggers a wave of depolarisation.

Carry the Signal Deep Inside via T-tubules**
Striated muscle fibres are thick, so surface depolarisation alone would be too slow to reach central myofibrils. Transverse system tubules (T-tubules) are infoldings of sarcolemma that run deep into the fibre. They conduct the depolarisation rapidly inwards to every part of the fibre almost simultaneously.

Release Internal Calcium from the Sarcoplasmic Reticulum**
Depolarisation of T-tubules depolarises the adjacent sarcoplasmic reticulum membrane. This opens voltage-gated calcium ion channels in the SR, so Ca2+ stored at high concentration in the SR cisternae diffuse out into the sarcoplasm. The rise in cytoplasmic Ca2+ allows Ca2+ to bind troponin, moving tropomyosin and starting cross-bridge cycling and contraction.

Final answer: Action potential depolarises presynaptic membrane; voltage-gated calcium ion channels open and Ca2+ enter presynaptic knob; vesicles fuse with presynaptic membrane and acetylcholine released by exocytosis into synaptic cleft; ACh binds receptors on sarcolemma / motor end plate; sodium ion channels open and Na+ enter causing depolarisation of sarcolemma; depolarisation spreads down T-tubules to sarcoplasmic reticulum; voltage-gated Ca2+ channels in SR open and Ca2+ diffuse into sarcoplasm to bind troponin and initiate contraction.

walkthrough:
Genetics - Dominant Allele on an Autosome**
Huntington's is caused by a mutant allele of the huntingtin gene on chromosome 4, which is an autosome. It is dominant, so only one copy is needed for the phenotype to appear. That is why it appears every generation and affects males and females equally.

Mutation - CAG Repeat Expansion**
The mutation is a trinucleotide repeat expansion of CAG. A normal recessive allele has 10-35 CAG repeats. The mutant dominant allele has more than this, often 36+. There is a clear dosage effect: the larger the number of repeats, the earlier the onset and often the more severe the course.

Age of Onset Pattern**
Usual onset is in middle age, typically after about 28 years and before 65, so symptoms often appear after reproduction. If repeats are very numerous, onset can be in childhood, even from about 1 year old (juvenile Huntington's).

Protein Effect - Misfolded Huntingtin**
CAG codes for glutamine, so extra repeats produce a polyglutamine tract and a misfolded huntingtin protein. The misfolded protein aggregates and is toxic, especially to neurones in the brain, first in the basal ganglia and striatum, including GABA-producing neurones. Neurones die and brain tissue is lost.

Phenotype - Loss of Control**
Because the basal ganglia normally inhibit unwanted movement, neurone loss leaves motor control uninhibited, giving chorea - rapid involuntary jerky movements - plus loss of coordination. There are also cognitive decline and mood / personality changes, progressing to severe neurodegeneration.

Final answer: Mutation in gene on chromosome 4 / autosome; dominant allele so one copy causes disease; normal allele has 10-35 CAG repeats, mutant HD allele has extra / more CAG repeats; greater number of repeats gives earlier onset; usual onset in middle age after 28 years, very large expansions cause onset from 1 year old; extra CAG gives polyglutamine tract causing misfolded huntingtin protein; brain neurones, especially in basal ganglia / striatum, die; loss of motor inhibition causes chorea / involuntary movements plus cognitive and mood changes.
